title: A trim handle can be pulled past a cut when you mean to
goal: Trimming a recording, a handle now catches on every cut it passes, which is what makes trimming exactly to a cut easy. The cost is that the band around each cut became unreachable: while the magnet is on you cannot park a handle within eight points of a cut by dragging at all. The canvas already has the answer for this and teaches it everywhere else, which is to hold a key and the magnet lets go for that drag. Give the trim handles the same key, so catching helps you instead of fencing you in.
notes:
From the rough list of queue/audits/2026-09-17-video-cutting-trim-catch.json, which names both the problem and this fix: while the magnet is on you cannot park a handle inside eight points of a cut, those positions are unreachable by dragging, and a modifier key to free the magnet mid-drag, the way the canvas uses Command, was left out as the shortest thing that delivers the value and is the obvious next move if that band turns out to matter.

No card: this is the canvas idiom already in the app, applied to a control the user already has, not a new gesture invented here. Find what the canvas actually uses and match it rather than picking a key.

The audit also says the precise way in already exists, which is parking the playhead and pressing I or O, and neither of those snaps. That is the argument for calling this p2 rather than p1: there is a way to land in the band, it is just not the way your hand is already on.

Files: Sources/Photonz/TrimTimeline.swift and the magnet in the trim drag path; the canvas magnet defeat key is the thing to copy. Not reproduced by hand: the Mac has been locked since 2026-09-15 so no walk runs; the audit measured it by test.
acceptance: Holding the same modifier the canvas uses to defeat its magnets frees a trim handle mid-drag: the handle follows the pointer exactly and catches on nothing.
Letting the key go mid-drag turns catching back on without the handle jumping.
Pressing the key after the drag has already started works, not only before, so you reach for it at the moment you find you cannot land where you want.
The handle tooltip or the trim row says the key, the way the other buttons on that row name theirs.
The magnet numbers themselves are unchanged: 8 points to reach, 16 to hold.

Try it: Photonz Dev, release Next. Open a recording, press T for trim, drag a handle towards a cut and watch it catch, then drag again with the key held and park it 3 points short of the cut. The flag is the one a-trim-handle-catches-on-a-cut-as-it-passes shipped behind; name it in the audit.
anything left rough is filed as a follow-up task if it clears the follow-up bar, and written into this task´s log if it does not

log.note: Adversarial review before building. (1) THE ONE REAL CONFLICT: the canvas key is Command, but on the canvas it LATCHES -- SnapHold.free() turns the magnets off and never back on for the rest of that drag, because "a magnet that came back when the key came up would move the thing you had just placed by hand". Acceptance item 2 asks for the opposite: let the key go mid-drag and catching comes back, without the handle jumping. Taken literally the canvas behaviour fails item 2 and the acceptance fails the canvas. Building item 2, with the canvas's own reason honoured by a different mechanism: on key-up, every cut within the 8pt reach is MUTED until the hand has travelled 16pt clear of it (the same dead band a caught cut already uses to hold). So nothing can yank the handle, which is the whole point of the latch, and yet the NEXT cut along still catches -- which on a one-axis track is usually the one you were heading for anyway. Latching would have made the key a one-shot per drag, and a trim drag passes several cuts. (2) Discovery: nothing on screen says Command frees it, so the handle gets a tooltip naming the key the way the row's buttons name theirs. (3) Collision check: the video controller itself is draggable, but the handle's own gesture is on top and Command-drag hits nothing else in that window. (4) Shortest version: no new key, no new chrome, no change to the 8/16 numbers -- one flag carried down the existing drag path into a hold that lives in PhotonzCore. Rejected: a toggle button for the magnet (a mode you can leave switched wrong), and a separate "snap to cuts" setting (a preference for a thing the hand should decide per drag).

Adversarial review of the built thing, on the real app. (1) A row pill reading "⌘ ignores cuts", shown only while a handle is caught, was built and taken back out: the transport cluster is drawn CENTRED over the same strip that carries the status labels, so the pill ran straight into the play button. Photographed before removing it. The handle tooltip carries the key instead, which is the acceptance's own first option. (2) The tooltip revealed a real bug in how a tooltip is hung: the handles are placed with SwiftUI's `offset`, which moves what is DRAWN without moving what was laid out, and a tooltip hangs off a real AppKit view laid over the control. Measured with three hovers at three different handle positions: all three came up at the same place, the left edge of the window, naming a handle that was not there. Fixed by hanging each handle's tooltip on its own invisible sibling placed with `position` (which tracks: 6, 640, 145 for three positions), and the handle itself is byte-for-byte the drag path it was, so nothing about the gesture changed. (3) I got this wrong once on the way: I "verified" the position fix with `playtest.sh --no-build`, which runs the PREVIOUS probe binary, and read the unchanged result as proof the fix had not worked. --no-build is for walks you have not rebuilt for.

left rough (each is a line of queue/audits/2026-09-17-video-cutting-trim-free.json that the user can react to, which files a task by their hand; none clears the follow-up bar on its own): (a) the row has nowhere to put a permanent hint because the transport is centred over the status labels -- not filed, because nothing SHIPPED collides there and an unreproduced crowding problem is not a bug; (b) the ⌘ read itself is the one link no test covers, because a SwiftUI drag carries no modifiers so the app reads NSEvent.modifierFlags at event time, and a walk has no hand on the keyboard; (c) the tell for the freed state is subtractive -- the lit slot simply stops being drawn -- so pressing the key away from any cut says nothing; (d) the slot lingers one frame past the key going down, since the key is read per drag event and a stationary press moves nothing; (e) three points short of a cut looks identical to being on it, and what tells you is the timecode gaining hundredths and the piece count going 2 of 3 to 3 of 3; (f) the magnet runs outside the cutting flag -- an uncut recording's two ends catch too -- which was true before this change and is untouched by it.
